newsitem.title: INDIA: Kashmir separatists want to be part of peace talks.
newsitem.headline: Kashmir separatists want to be part of peace talks.

text.p: Kashmiri separatists on Tuesday cautiously welcomed India's agreement to discuss the divided region in talks with Pakistan but urged the two nations to include Kashmiris in the negotiations.
"I am happy that India has finally agreed to talk over the Kashmir dispute," separatist leader Shabir Ahmad Shah told Reuters in the summer capital of Jammu and Kashmir state, Srinagar.

"It is a healthy sign, but these two neighbours in future talks must include Kashmiris, main party to the dispute, for better results," said Shah, one of the most popular separatist leaders in the state.

India maintains that Kashmir, including a section controlled by Pakistan since 1947, is an integral part of the union, and insists that any discussions be limited to representatives of New Delhi and Islamabad.
High-ranking officials from India and Pakistan agreed on Monday in Islamabad to set up working groups to tackle all outstanding issues dividing the longtime foes.

"Though India has agreed to talk over Kashmir, we are sure without participation of real representatives of both sides of Kashmir the dialogue between these two countries over disputed Kashmir will lead nowhere," Umar Farooq, chairman of the All Parties Hurriyat (Freedom) Conference, told Reuters.
The Hurriyat includes nearly 30 separatist groups.
"If India is serious about talks over Kashmir they should first stop their security forces who are committing human rights violations in Kashmir," Farooq said.

The chief minister of Jammu and Kashmir, Farooq Abdullah, on Saturday called on Pakistan to stop its "proxy war" in Kashmir and turn over the one third of the region which Islamabad controls to India.
India accuses Pakistan of arming and training guerrillas who launched a separatist rebellion in 1990. Police and hospital officials say more than 20,000 have died in the revolt.
Mohammad Shafi Bhat, a lawmaker and leader of Abdullah's ruling National Conference party, called Monday's agreement between India and Pakistan a welcome step.

"I think in the future, only a change of the line of actual control into international border will bring peace to the subcontinent," he said, referring to the interim boundary which has divided Kashmir for nearly 50 years.

"It is a positive development, but there must be a sincere and realistic approach to this problem, to try to find out a solution acceptable to both the countries," M. Yusuf Tarigami, state leader of the Communist Party of India (Marxist), said.
